parts.context: Two friends are dealing with a problem the evening before one of them moves to a new apartment.

lines: Gareth, sorry to call so late. The moving company just phoned. Their truck failed a safety inspection this afternoon, and they can’t do tomorrow’s job. They offered me Thursday instead.
Thursday? But your lease on Dundas ends tomorrow at midnight, doesn’t it?

Technically, yes. And it’s not just that. The new building only gave me the service elevator from nine to one tomorrow. I had to book it three weeks ago, and the property manager told me there are no other openings until the end of the month.
Okay, so two deadlines. Could you ask your current landlord for a couple of extra days?

I tried, actually. I texted him right after the movers called. He was polite about it, but the new tenants are bringing their own things in on Wednesday morning, and the painters are coming in between. He said if I’m still there Wednesday, he’d have to charge me a full extra month.
A full month? For two days? That seems a bit much.

That’s what I said, but it’s written into the lease, and honestly, I don’t want to start a fight with him when I need my damage deposit back. It’s eleven hundred dollars, and I was counting on it for the first month at the new place.
Fair enough. Did the movers at least offer you anything for the trouble?
They’ll refund my deposit, the two hundred, but that’s it. Everything else is on me. I spent twenty minutes on hold just to hear that.
Unbelievable. Okay, let’s not panic. We’ve got tonight and the whole morning. Let’s figure out what’s actually possible.

qs.q: Why can the moving company not do the job tomorrow?
o: Their vehicle was found to be unfit for the road.
They accidentally booked the truck for another client.
The new building cancelled Noor’s elevator booking.
They want Noor to pay a larger deposit first.
qs.ev: Their truck failed a safety inspection this afternoon
qs.x: A truck that “failed a safety inspection” cannot be driven safely. The elevator booking is still in place (nine to one), and the deposit is being refunded, not increased.

qs.q: What would happen if Noor stayed in her old apartment until Wednesday?
o: She would lose her damage deposit.
The painters would charge her for the delay.
She would owe her landlord an additional month’s rent.
The new tenants would move in around her.
qs.ev: he’d have to charge me a full extra month
qs.x: The landlord said he would “charge me a full extra month” if she stayed until Wednesday. The damage deposit is something she wants back, not something he threatened to keep.

qs.q: Why does Noor not want to argue with her landlord?
o: She thinks the extra charge is reasonable.
He has already agreed to delay the painters.
She is afraid he will refuse to give her a reference.
She is worried it could affect money he owes her.
qs.ev: I don’t want to start a fight with him when I need my damage deposit back
qs.x: She needs her $1,100 deposit returned, so a dispute could put that money at risk. She actually agrees with Gareth that the charge is too much (“That’s what I said”).

lines: What about renting a truck yourself? I could drive. I moved my sister last year with one of those sixteen-foot ones.
I looked. Every truck in the city is booked because it’s the end of the month. The closest one is in Milton, and they close at six tonight.
Hmm, Milton’s an hour each way. And even if we got there, I can’t carry a fridge and a sofa down three flights with just the two of us.
Exactly. The fridge stays, thankfully. It belongs to the unit. But the sofa and the bed, there’s no way.
What about one of those apps where you book a van and a driver by the hour? My coworker used one when she moved out of her basement suite.

I checked that too. They have a driver free from eight to noon, but the biggest vehicle they’ve got is a cargo van. My stuff would take at least three trips, and the new place is forty minutes away in traffic.
So you’d run out of elevator time before the third load.
That’s my fear. Unless, what if we split it up? The van takes the big furniture first, while the elevator’s booked, and the boxes come over later in cars. Boxes can go up the regular elevator, right?
That depends on the building. Some places don’t let you move anything through the main lobby at all.
I’ll double-check the rules on the residents’ portal. I think the rule was only about furniture, but I’m not certain.

qs.q: Why does Gareth think renting a truck would not work?
o: The rental office in Milton has already closed.
Two people could not manage the heaviest items alone.
He has never driven a vehicle of that size.
The truck would have to make three separate trips.
qs.ev: I can’t carry a fridge and a sofa down three flights with just the two of us
qs.x: Gareth says the two of them cannot carry the large furniture down three flights. The Milton office closes at six but is not yet closed, and he has driven such a truck before.

qs.q: What worries Noor about the van service?
o: The driver is only available in the afternoon.
The van is too small to carry her sofa.
The service costs more than the original movers.
The move might not fit within her reserved elevator time.
qs.ev: So you’d run out of elevator time before the third load
qs.x: When Gareth says they would run out of elevator time, Noor answers “That’s my fear.” The driver is free in the morning (eight to noon), and the van’s size means more trips, not that the sofa will not fit.

qs.q: What is Noor unsure about?
o: Whether her coworker’s app is still operating
Whether the van driver will help carry furniture
Whether boxes are allowed through the building’s entrance
Whether the fridge belongs to her or the landlord
qs.ev: I think the rule was only about furniture, but I’m not certain
qs.x: She is not sure whether the lobby rule covers boxes or only furniture. The app belongs to Gareth’s coworker’s experience, and she is certain the fridge belongs to the unit.

lines: Okay, I’ve got the building rules open. Boxes in the main elevator are fine as long as they’re on a dolly and it’s after ten a.m. on weekdays. Furniture only goes in the service elevator.
Great, so the plan works. Van for the furniture from eight, cars for the boxes after ten.

Wait, though. The van driver starts at my old place at eight, loading takes maybe an hour, and then it’s forty minutes of driving. He’d get to the new place at around ten to ten. That only leaves us about three hours of service elevator.
That’s plenty for a sofa, a bed and a dresser. And if we finish early, we can use the service elevator for boxes too.
True. Okay. I’ll book the van now. It’s sixty-five an hour with a four-hour minimum, which is still less than the movers were charging me.
And I’ll ask my brother if we can borrow his SUV. Between that and your hatchback, we should get all the boxes over in two trips.
You’re a lifesaver. I’ll buy pizza for everyone. Oh, and I should tell the movers I’m cancelling Thursday entirely, so they actually send the refund.
Get that in writing. Send them an email tonight, not just a phone call. Companies like that have a way of forgetting conversations.
Good point. I’ll do it the second we hang up, and I’ll copy you so there’s a witness.

qs.q: When may boxes be taken up in the main elevator?
o: On a moving cart, from mid-morning onward
Only before the furniture arrives at ten to ten
Only during the service elevator booking
At any time, as long as they are carried by hand
qs.ev: as long as they’re on a dolly and it’s after ten a.m. on weekdays
qs.x: A dolly is a moving cart, and “after ten a.m.” is mid-morning onward. “Ten to ten” is when the van arrives, and the service elevator is reserved for furniture.

qs.q: What does Gareth advise Noor to do?
o: Phone the movers tonight to request the refund
Keep a written record of the cancellation
Ask the movers to send the truck on Thursday
Copy her brother on all messages to the company
qs.ev: Get that in writing.
qs.x: He tells her to “get that in writing” by email rather than by phone, so she has a record. A phone call is exactly what he warns against, and it is Noor who offers to copy Gareth.

parts.context: A tenant is talking to the superintendent of her apartment building.

lines: Hi Kwame, have you got a second? It’s Rosalind from 704.
Sure, what’s up? Is the bathroom fan acting up again?

No, no, that’s been fine since you replaced it. It’s about packages. That’s the second one that’s gone missing from the lobby this month. A pair of boots on the ninth, and yesterday a birthday present for my nephew.

Ugh, I’m sorry. You’re not the only one. I’ve had four complaints this week. The problem is the side door by the recycling room. The latch doesn’t catch properly, so when it’s windy the door blows open and anybody can walk in.
I wondered about that. I’ve seen it propped open with a brick a couple of times, too.

That’s the movers and some of the delivery drivers. I take the brick away every time, believe me. Anyway, the new latch is ordered. The supplier said ten business days, but they said that last time and it took three weeks, so I’m not holding my breath.
In the meantime, is there anything I can do? I order a lot online for work.

A couple of things. The management office takes packages from nine to five on weekdays, so you can put the office down as your delivery address. Just write “care of the office” and your unit number. They keep things for seven days.
The trouble is I work until six. I’d never get there in time.
Right. Then there’s the parcel locker at the pharmacy on the corner. It’s free, you get a code by text, and it’s open until eleven at night.
Oh, I didn’t know about that one. I’ll try it. Honestly, though, shouldn’t the building have its own lockers? The place I lived in before had them.
You’re preaching to the choir. I’ve suggested it twice. The owners say it’s on the list for next year’s budget, but between you and me, they said that last year as well.
Well, would it help if tenants wrote to them directly?
It couldn’t hurt. If a dozen people put it in writing, it’s harder to push down the list. And please file a report for the boots and the present, so there’s a record of what’s been taken.

qs.q: Why did Rosalind want to speak to Kwame?
o: Her bathroom fan has stopped working again.
A door near her unit no longer locks.
Things delivered to her have disappeared.
She wants to complain about some delivery drivers.
qs.ev: That’s the second one that’s gone missing from the lobby this month
qs.x: Two of her packages have “gone missing” from the lobby – deliveries have disappeared. The fan was fixed, and the faulty side door is by the recycling room, not near her unit.

qs.q: What does Kwame suggest about the new latch?
o: He doubts it will arrive as quickly as promised.
It will take about three weeks to install.
He has already received it from the supplier.
It will not stop people from propping the door.
qs.ev: so I’m not holding my breath
qs.x: “Not holding my breath” means he does not expect it on time, because the supplier was late before. Three weeks was the delay last time, not the installation time.

qs.q: Why is the management office not a practical choice for Rosalind?
o: It keeps parcels for only a few days.
It does not accept deliveries for tenants.
It charges a fee to hold packages.
Its hours do not suit her work schedule.
qs.ev: The trouble is I work until six.
qs.x: The office closes at five, but she works until six, so she could not collect parcels. The office does accept tenant parcels and keeps them for seven days.

qs.q: How does Kwame feel about the idea of building lockers?
o: He thinks the pharmacy locker makes them unnecessary.
He supports them but doubts the owners’ commitment.
He expects them to be installed next year.
He worries they would be too costly to maintain.
qs.ev: You’re preaching to the choir.
qs.x: “Preaching to the choir” means he already agrees, but he hints the owners made the same promise last year. So he does not really expect them next year.

qs.q: What will Rosalind most likely do today?
o: Change her delivery address to the management office
Ask a dozen tenants to meet with the owners
Write to the owners and report the missing items
Remove the brick from the side door herself
qs.ev: I’ll do both today.
qs.x: “Both” refers to writing to the owners and filing a report on the lost boots and present. The office address does not suit her hours, and Kwame, not she, removes the brick.

parts.context: A man calls a tenant information line with questions about subletting his apartment.

lines: Tenant Information Line, this is Margaret. How can I help?

Hi. I rent a one-bedroom on the east side, and I’ve been offered a six-month work contract in Calgary starting in February. I don’t want to give up the apartment, because the rent is really reasonable for the area, so I was thinking of subletting it. Is that allowed?

In most cases, yes. The key thing is that you need your landlord’s consent in writing before anyone moves in. You make the request, and the landlord has thirty days to respond. If they don’t reply at all within that time, you can treat the request as refused, not approved, and then you can apply to the tenancy board.
Oh. I would’ve assumed no answer meant yes.

A lot of people think that. It’s actually the opposite. Now, a landlord can’t refuse without a good reason. For example, they can check the subtenant’s references and refuse someone with a history of not paying, but they can’t refuse just because they’d prefer to re-rent the unit at a higher rate.
Okay. And how much can I charge the person? I’m leaving all my furniture.

The rule is that you cannot charge the subtenant more than you pay. You can ask for a reasonable amount to cover utilities if those aren’t included in your rent, but furniture doesn’t change the limit.
Hmm. That’s fair, I suppose. What happens if the person damages something or stops paying?

That’s the part people underestimate. You’re still the tenant. So if the subtenant misses the rent, the landlord comes to you, and you’d be responsible for any damage beyond normal wear and tear. We strongly recommend a written agreement between you and the subtenant, and a deposit. You’re allowed to collect up to one month’s rent for that.
And when I come back, the subtenant has to leave?

As long as the agreement has a clear end date, yes. If they refuse to go, you can apply to the board to have them removed. That process can take six to eight weeks, so some people build in a cushion. They end the sublet two weeks before they’re actually due back.
That’s smart. One more thing. A friend told me I should just call it an assignment instead. Is that the same thing?

No, and this is important. An assignment means you give up the lease permanently. The new person becomes the tenant, and you have no right to return. If you plan to come back, a sublet is what you want.
Got it. Can you send me something in writing?
Of course. I’ll email you our sublet checklist and a sample consent request letter. What’s the best address for you?

qs.q: Why does the caller want to keep his apartment?
o: His contract in Calgary may be cancelled.
He might not find a comparable price later.
He has nowhere else to store his furniture.
His landlord has asked him to find a replacement.
qs.ev: the rent is really reasonable for the area
qs.x: A “really reasonable” rent implies he would struggle to find something similar if he gave the apartment up. Furniture is mentioned only regarding what he can charge.

qs.q: What happens if the landlord does not reply within thirty days?
o: The sublet is approved automatically.
The tenancy board contacts the landlord.
The caller must wait another thirty days.
The caller should consider the answer a no.
qs.ev: you can treat the request as refused, not approved
qs.x: Silence counts as a refusal, which the caller can then challenge at the board. The tempting option – automatic approval – is exactly the mistake the advisor corrects.

qs.q: Which reason would allow a landlord to reject a proposed subtenant?
o: The person has failed to pay rent in the past.
The landlord could earn more from a new tenant.
The apartment will be rented with furniture.
The caller will be away for more than six months.
qs.ev: refuse someone with a history of not paying
qs.x: A “history of not paying” is a valid reason. Wanting a higher rate is specifically named as an unacceptable reason.

qs.q: What does the advisor say about the amount the subtenant pays?
o: It may include an extra charge for furniture.
It must cover all of the utilities.
It may not be higher than the caller’s own rent.
It is limited to one month paid in advance.
qs.ev: you cannot charge the subtenant more than you pay
qs.x: The subtenant cannot pay more than the caller pays. Furniture “doesn’t change the limit”, and one month is the maximum deposit, not a rule about rent.

qs.q: Why do some tenants end a sublet two weeks early?
o: To clean the unit before the landlord inspects it
To have time to return the subtenant’s deposit
To make sure the board approves the agreement
To allow for delays if the subtenant will not leave
qs.ev: so some people build in a cushion
qs.x: Removing a subtenant through the board can take six to eight weeks, so the extra two weeks is a buffer. Cleaning and deposits are not mentioned as reasons.

qs.q: What would happen if the caller chose an assignment?
o: He would give up any right to move back in.
His landlord would have to approve his return.
His friend would become responsible for the rent.
He would remain liable for any damage.
qs.ev: you have no right to return
qs.x: An assignment ends the caller’s tenancy permanently. Remaining liable for damage applies to a sublet, which is the trap here.

parts.context: You will hear a local news report.

lines: Landlords in Fairhaven will soon need a licence to rent out apartments. City council voted nine to four last night to approve a rental licensing program, the first of its kind in the region. Starting in April, owners of any building with four or more rental units will have to register with the city, pay an annual fee of fifteen dollars per unit, and pass a basic inspection every two years. Buildings with a history of complaints could be inspected every year.

The vote follows a report last spring that found more than a third of the city’s older apartment buildings had at least one outstanding safety issue, from broken fire doors to elevators that had been out of service for months. Under the current system, inspectors only visit when a tenant files a complaint, and many tenants told the city they were afraid to do so.
Delphine Osei of the Fairhaven Tenants’ Alliance has been pushing for licensing for nearly five years.

Honestly, it’s a relief. For years, the whole system depended on tenants complaining about the person who decides whether their lease gets renewed. That’s not a fair position to put anyone in. Now the city goes in on a schedule, whether or not anyone has spoken up. Is the fee perfect? No. I’d have liked to see it higher, to pay for more inspectors. But it’s a start.

Not everyone is celebrating. The Fairhaven Landlords’ Association argues the program punishes responsible owners for the actions of a few, and warns that the cost of fees and repairs will eventually show up in tenants’ rents. Council members who voted against the bylaw raised a different concern: the city currently employs only six property standards inspectors, and the program’s first-year budget funds just four more.

City staff say small landlords who rent out a basement apartment or a single house are exempt, at least for now. Council has asked for a report in eighteen months on whether to extend the program to smaller properties.

qs.q: What will the new program require?
o: Yearly inspections of every rental unit in the city
Licences for homeowners who rent out a basement
A fee of fifteen dollars for each building
Regular checks of larger rental buildings
qs.ev: pass a basic inspection every two years
qs.x: Buildings with four or more units must pass an inspection every two years. Yearly checks apply only to buildings with complaints, basement rentals are exempt, and the fee is per unit.

qs.q: According to the report, why did the existing system fail?
o: Inspectors visited only once every two years.
Tenants were reluctant to report problems.
Older buildings were not covered by the rules.
Elevator repairs were the owners’ responsibility.
qs.ev: many tenants told the city they were afraid to do so
qs.x: Inspections depended on complaints, and tenants were afraid to complain. “Every two years” describes the new program, not the old one.

qs.q: How does Delphine Osei feel about the fee?
o: She accepts it, though she would have preferred more.
She fears it will be passed on to tenants.
She thinks it is unfair to small landlords.
She considers it the most important part of the bylaw.
qs.ev: I’d have liked to see it higher
qs.x: She says the fee is not perfect and should be higher, but “it’s a start” – qualified acceptance. Passing costs to tenants is the landlords’ argument.

qs.q: What concern did the councillors who voted against the bylaw raise?
o: Responsible owners would be punished unfairly.
Rents would rise to cover repair costs.
The city may lack the staff to enforce it.
Tenants were not consulted before the vote.
qs.ev: the program’s first-year budget funds just four more
qs.x: They pointed out that the city has only six inspectors and the budget adds just four. Unfair punishment and higher rents are the landlords’ association’s arguments.

qs.q: What may happen in the future?
o: The annual fee could be raised to hire inspectors.
Smaller rental properties could be included.
Basement apartments will be inspected every year.
The program could be cancelled after eighteen months.
qs.ev: whether to extend the program to smaller properties
qs.x: Council asked for a report on extending licensing to smaller properties. A higher fee is only Osei’s wish, and nothing suggests cancelling the program.

parts.context: Three members of a condominium board are discussing how to pay for a major repair.

lines: Okay, let’s get to the main item. The engineer’s report is clear: the windows on the north and west sides are failing. Condensation, drafts, and in two units, water is getting into the walls. Replacing all of them is estimated at one point two million.

And our reserve fund has about four hundred thousand, which we can’t empty, because the roof is due in six years. So, as treasurer, I’ll say it plainly: I think we need a special assessment. Spread across ninety units, it works out to roughly nine thousand dollars per unit, depending on size.
I’d propose two instalments, six months apart.

Colette, I understand the math, but you know who lives here. At least a quarter of our owners are retired. Mrs. Abebe on the fourth floor told me last week she’s already struggling with the fee increase from January. Asking her for nine thousand dollars in one year could force her to sell.
I don’t take that lightly. But every year we wait, the price goes up. The engineer said material costs rose eleven percent last year alone. And the water damage in those two units is going to spread.
Then why not do it in phases? North side first, since that’s where the leaks are, and the west side in three or four years when the reserve has recovered.

I asked the engineer about phasing, actually. He said it’s possible, but we’d pay for scaffolding and permits twice, which adds about fifteen percent. And there’s a warranty issue: the contractor would only guarantee a matching product for two years.
Hmm. So the west side might end up with different windows. That’s not ideal, but I could live with it.
I couldn’t. Mismatched windows will hurt resale values for everyone, and buyers’ inspectors will ask questions.

Let me put a third option on the table. Some buildings are taking out a loan for this kind of project. The corporation borrows the money and repays it over ten or fifteen years through the monthly fees. Nobody has to come up with a lump sum.
How much would fees go up?
The broker I spoke to estimated around ninety dollars a month for an average unit, over twelve years.
That’s a lot of interest in total. We’d end up paying far more than one point two million.
True. But owners who want to avoid the interest could pay their share up front. The broker said that’s quite common, a kind of opt-out.
Huh. I hadn’t considered that combination. That would let people like me pay now, and give Mrs. Abebe a manageable monthly amount.

Ninety dollars a month is still real money for some people, but it’s a whole lot more realistic than nine thousand at once. I’d support that, as long as we hold an information session before anybody votes.
Fine by me. But I want the engineer at that session. If owners hear about the water in the walls from him and not from us, they’ll take it seriously.

Agreed. So we’ll recommend a full replacement funded by a loan, with an option to pay up front, and we’ll hold an owners’ information session with the engineer next month, before the vote at the general meeting.
And let’s get quotes from at least two other lenders. I don’t want to go with the first broker who called us back.
Fair enough. I’ll handle that this week.

qs.q: Why can the board not pay for the windows from the reserve fund?
o: The engineer advised against touching it.
Owners voted last year to freeze it.
Part of it must be kept for another major repair.
It was set aside for the two damaged units.
qs.ev: the roof is due in six years
qs.x: Colette says they cannot empty the fund because the roof will need replacing in six years. The engineer’s advice concerned phasing, not the reserve fund.

qs.q: Why does Owen object to a special assessment?
o: Many owners could not afford a large payment.
He believes the engineer exaggerated the damage.
He thinks January’s fee increase was enough.
He would prefer to sell his own unit first.
qs.ev: Asking her for nine thousand dollars in one year could force her to sell
qs.x: He uses Mrs. Abebe and the many retired owners to show that a lump sum would be unaffordable. It is Mrs. Abebe, not Owen, who might have to sell.

qs.q: What argument does Colette use for acting quickly?
o: Material costs will rise eleven percent next year.
The roof and windows should be replaced together.
Owners will be more willing to pay this year.
Waiting will make the project more expensive.
qs.ev: every year we wait, the price goes up
qs.x: She says the price rises every year they wait. The eleven percent rise happened last year; she does not predict that figure for next year.

qs.q: What drawback of phasing did the engineer mention?
o: The north side would have to wait several years.
Some costs would have to be paid a second time.
The windows would need new permits every two years.
The contractor would refuse to provide a warranty.
qs.ev: we’d pay for scaffolding and permits twice
qs.x: Scaffolding and permits would be paid for twice, adding about fifteen percent. The warranty is limited to matching products for two years, not refused.

qs.q: How does Owen feel about the possibility of mismatched windows?
o: He sees them as an acceptable compromise.
He thinks they would lower property values.
He believes buyers’ inspectors would object.
He wants the contractor to guarantee a match.
qs.ev: That’s not ideal, but I could live with it.
qs.x: “Not ideal, but I could live with it” shows reluctant acceptance. Concerns about resale values and inspectors are Colette’s, not Owen’s.

qs.q: What is Colette’s first reaction to the loan idea?
o: She doubts the bank would approve the loan.
She thinks the monthly increase is too high.
She objects to the overall cost of borrowing.
She worries that owners will refuse to vote.
qs.ev: That’s a lot of interest in total.
qs.x: She objects that interest would make the total much more than $1.2 million. It is Owen who comments that ninety dollars a month is “real money”.

qs.q: What makes Colette change her mind about the loan?
o: The broker offers a lower interest rate.
The repayment period is shorter than expected.
The engineer agrees to attend the session.
Owners could choose to pay their portion immediately.
qs.ev: owners who want to avoid the interest could pay their share up front
qs.x: The opt-out lets owners like her avoid interest while others pay monthly – “I hadn’t considered that combination.” The engineer’s attendance is her later condition, not the reason she changed her mind.

qs.q: What will Harjit do this week?
o: Book the engineer for the information session
Look for additional loan offers
Schedule the owners’ vote for next month
Ask the broker to lower the monthly amount
qs.ev: let’s get quotes from at least two other lenders
qs.x: Owen asks for quotes from two other lenders, and Harjit says he will handle it. Next month is the information session; the vote is at the general meeting.

parts.context: You will hear a radio report about a change to local housing rules.

lines: For most of the last century, the rules in Canadian suburbs have been simple: on most residential streets, you can build one house per lot, and that’s it. That’s now changing. Several cities, including ours, have voted to allow up to four homes on any residential lot, whether as a fourplex, a house with a basement suite and a garden home, or some other combination. Supporters call it the “missing middle”: housing that sits between the detached house and the high-rise tower.

Urban planner Ines Vachon has studied the policy in three cities. She argues it’s less about any single building than about who gets to live in established neighbourhoods. In her words, if a teacher or a nurse can’t afford a whole house near a good school, perhaps they can afford a third of one. She also points out that these areas often have schools with empty classrooms and bus routes with plenty of spare capacity, so the infrastructure is already paid for.

Not everyone is convinced. At a packed public meeting last month, residents raised concerns about parking, the loss of mature trees and new buildings casting shadows over backyards. Retired engineer Paul Szabo, who has lived on the same street for thirty-one years, told me he isn’t against newcomers, but he resents what he sees as a decision made without real consultation. He says the city held one meeting after the vote, not before it, and that the old rules were what people relied on when they bought their homes.

Economists, meanwhile, are cautious about the promises on both sides. Housing economist Farah Lindqvist says opponents who predict a wave of fourplexes on every street are likely to be disappointed, or relieved, depending on their point of view. Her research suggests that in cities that made similar changes, only a small share of lots were redeveloped in the first five years. Building a fourplex, she notes, often costs as much per unit as a condo, because land is expensive and construction costs have soared. Her conclusion: the reform is necessary, but on its own it is too modest to make a real dent in prices.

Some builders agree, but for a different reason. Small developer Kofi Mensah, who has built six fourplexes since the rules changed, says the zoning is the easy part. What slows him down is everything else: development fees that are the same for a fourplex as for four detached houses, and a permit process that can take more than a year. He says that if the city wants more of these buildings, it should cut the fees and speed up approvals, not just redraw the map.
For now, the city says it will review the policy in two years and report on how many new homes it has actually produced.

qs.q: According to Ines Vachon, what is the main benefit of the policy?
o: People with moderate incomes could live in established areas.
Teachers and nurses would be able to buy detached houses.
Schools would be able to reduce class sizes.
Cities could pay for new bus routes in the suburbs.

p1.meta: From: Bettina Kraus | To: Sunil Varma | Subject: News from Pembrook (and a favour)
p1.text:
Dear Sunil,

It’s been far too long since I last wrote, and I’m sorry I missed your call on Sunday. Things have been, let’s say, eventful. As you know, Marc and I finally took possession of the house in Pembrook at the start of September. I still love it: the big maple out front, the creaky stairs, the view of the river from the back bedroom. But owning a hundred-year-old house has turned out to be a very different thing from admiring one.

Three weeks in, our insurance company sent someone to do an inspection, and he found that about half the house still has the original wiring, the kind with ceramic knobs and tubes inside the walls. Our home inspector, before we bought, had flagged it as “possible older wiring, further investigation recommended”, and I’ll admit we were so excited that we skimmed right past that line. Now the insurer says they will only renew our policy in January if the wiring is replaced, and they want proof from a licensed electrician.

So the kitchen renovation we had planned for this fall is off. Every dollar we had set aside is going into the walls instead. The kitchen will have to wait until next spring, or possibly the spring after, depending on what the electrician finds once the walls are opened. Marc keeps joking that at least the cabinets are “vintage”. I am finding it a little less funny.

This is where you come in, if you’re willing. We have two quotes. One electrician, from right here in town, quoted $14,500 and can start in November. The other is from the city; he quoted $11,800 but can’t begin until mid-December, which cuts it very close to our renewal date. You’ve renovated three houses, and you have a much better eye for this sort of thing than either of us. Would you look at both quotes and tell me what you think? I can scan them tonight.

Also, we’ve had to postpone the housewarming. It was going to be Thanksgiving weekend, but there will be holes in half the walls by then. We’re now thinking of a winter party in late January, once the dust has literally settled. You and Leila are, of course, at the top of the list.

Warmly,
Bettina

p3.title: Living Together, Apart: The Return of Shared Housing
paras: In the early twentieth century, rooming houses were a common first stop for newcomers to Canadian cities: a private bedroom, a shared kitchen and bathroom, and a landlady who often lived on the premises. By the 1970s, many had been converted into single-family homes or closed after zoning changes, and the term itself came to suggest neglect. Today, a new generation of so-called co-living buildings is reviving the model under a more fashionable name. Residents rent a furnished private room, sometimes with its own small bathroom, and share a large kitchen, lounge and workspace. Operators handle the cleaning of common areas, internet and utilities, all bundled into one monthly price. The pitch is aimed squarely at young professionals who have just moved to a city for work and would rather not sign a twelve-month lease or buy a couch.

For residents, the appeal is often as much social as financial. Mireille Tan, a 27-year-old software tester, moved into a co-living building in Halifax after spending her first three months in the city in a basement apartment where, she says, she sometimes went a whole weekend without speaking to anyone. Her building hosts a weekly shared dinner and has a group chat that residents use to find hiking partners or borrow a ladle. Still, she is candid about the trade-offs. Her room is smaller than her old bedroom at her parents’ house, and the monthly price is only slightly lower than what a one-bedroom apartment would cost. “I’m paying for not being lonely,” she says. “Some months, that feels worth it. Other months, I do the math and wince.”

Critics are less charmed. Housing advocates point out that, per square metre, co-living rooms are frequently among the most expensive rentals in a city, and that operators can describe a modest room in glowing terms because each tenant signs a separate agreement and rarely compares notes. In some provinces, it is not even clear whether residents are covered by tenancy law at all, since they share kitchens with people who are not members of their family. That uncertainty matters most when something goes wrong: a resident who is asked to leave may struggle to find out what notice they are entitled to, or whom to complain to. Several advocates have asked governments to clarify the rules before the sector grows further, rather than after a wave of disputes.

Operators, for their part, argue that they are filling a gap the market has ignored. A co-living property, they say, uses land more efficiently than conventional one-bedroom apartments, because shared kitchens and living rooms replace dozens of private ones. Some municipalities have taken notice. One mid-sized city in Ontario recently allowed co-living buildings in areas zoned for apartments without requiring the parking spaces that a standard building would need, on the assumption that residents are less likely to own cars. Planners there describe it as an experiment; if it works, the same approach could be applied to student housing. Whether co-living becomes a permanent part of the housing mix or a passing trend may depend on how residents feel once the novelty of shared dinners wears off.

p4.title: It’s Time to End Blanket Pet Bans in Rental Housing
p4.byline: Opinion | by Leonard Pruitt, small landlord and housing columnist
p4.text:
Every spring, the animal shelter in my city sees the same sad wave. It is not puppies or kittens; it is grown dogs and middle-aged cats, surrendered by owners who could not find an apartment that would take them. Staff call it the “moving season surge”, and it peaks right around the first of July.

I have been a landlord for eleven years. I own two small buildings, fourteen units in total, and for the first five years, my leases said no pets, full stop. I believed what most landlords believe: that pets mean scratched floors, odours that never leave the carpet and complaints from the neighbours. Then a long-term tenant, a retired nurse who had never once been late with the rent, told me she would have to give up her cat or move out after her husband died. I made an exception. The sky did not fall.

Since then, I have allowed pets in every unit, and I have kept records. Over six years, the average pet-owning tenant has stayed with me for nearly four years; tenants without pets, for a little over two. Every turnover costs me a month or more of lost rent, plus cleaning and advertising. The damage, meanwhile, has been modest: one chewed door frame and two carpets replaced earlier than planned. I have spent more fixing holes left by tenants hanging heavy mirrors.

That is why I now support what would have seemed unthinkable to me a decade ago: a law making blanket no-pet clauses unenforceable in residential leases, as one province already does. Under such a law, landlords could still refuse a specific animal that is dangerous, or one that is clearly unsuitable for the unit, such as a large dog in a bachelor apartment. Condo buildings with their own bylaws would be a separate matter. But a landlord could no longer reject every tenant with a cat simply because it is easier.

I am not naive about the concerns. Allergies are real, and in older buildings with shared ventilation, an animal in one unit can affect another. Noise is real, too; a dog that barks for eight hours while its owner is at work is a genuine nuisance. But these are problems we already know how to handle. Noise is noise, whether it comes from a dog or a drum set, and tenancy law already allows a landlord to act when one tenant disturbs another. Allergies can be addressed through how units are cleaned between tenants.

What I would ask in return is a fair way to protect owners. The current rule in many provinces allows a landlord to collect a damage deposit of up to half a month’s rent, regardless of pets. I would allow an additional pet deposit, capped at, say, a quarter of a month’s rent, refundable in full if the unit is left in good condition. That is a modest cost for tenants and real reassurance for landlords, especially small ones who cannot absorb a large repair bill.

We are in a housing crisis, and we keep looking for complicated solutions. Here is a simple one that costs taxpayers nothing: let people bring their families with them, including the members with four legs. My buildings have quieter hallways and fewer vacancies than ever. I suspect most landlords would find the same, if the law gave them a reason to try.

t1.model:
Dear Ms. Albrecht,

I am writing about the washer on the left side of our building’s laundry room, which has been malfunctioning for about three weeks. It accepts payment through the card reader, but in roughly half of my recent loads it has stopped partway through, leaving my clothes soaking and locked inside for up to an hour. t2.intro: Your apartment building has a large empty room on the ground floor that used to be a storage area. The management company is asking tenants how the room should be used. Choose the option you prefer and explain your reasons.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer?
t2.a: Option A: Turn it into a small fitness room with two treadmills, an exercise bike and free weights, open from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. Each unit that uses it would pay $5 a month.
t2.b: Option B: Turn it into a quiet shared workspace with six desks, fast Wi-Fi and a small meeting room that residents can book. It would be free for everyone.
t2.model:
I would choose Option B, the shared workspace, for two main reasons.

First, it would serve far more residents. Since the pandemic, many people in our building work from home at least part of the week, and most of our units are one-bedroom apartments where the only “office” is a kitchen table. A quiet room with proper desks and fast Wi-Fi would make a real difference to people’s productivity and to their well-being. Students preparing for exams would also benefit, and the bookable meeting room would be ideal for anyone who needs privacy for an interview or a video call.

Second, it is fairer and simpler to run. Because the workspace would be free, no resident would be excluded, and management would not need to collect fees or track who is paying. A fitness room, by contrast, requires expensive equipment that breaks down, raises insurance concerns, and would mostly be used by a small group.

I understand the appeal of a gym on site, especially in winter. However, there are two affordable gyms within walking distance, whereas a quiet place to work is genuinely hard to find nearby.

t1.prompt: Your friend is thinking about buying a condominium in a building that has not been built yet. The developer says it will be finished in three years, and your friend would pay a deposit now. Your friend currently rents. Advise your friend about what to consider before signing.
t1.model:
I can see why you’re excited. Buying before construction often means a lower price, and you’d get a brand-new unit. But before you sign anything, I’d think about a few things.

First, the timeline. Three years is what the developer says, but delays of a year or more are really common, especially when construction costs go up. So ask yourself whether you could keep renting longer than planned, and check what the contract says if the project is delayed or even cancelled. You want to know your deposit is protected, ideally in a trust account.

Second, think about your budget in three years, not just today. Interest rates could be higher when you actually need the mortgage, and new condos often come with closing costs and occupancy fees that people forget about. I’d talk to a mortgage advisor first.

Third, look into the developer’s track record. Have they finished other buildings on time? Are owners in those buildings happy, or are there complaints about quality?

And finally, have a real estate lawyer review the agreement before you sign. Most provinces give you a cooling-off period, so you’d have a few days to back out if something looks wrong. Honestly, I’m not saying don’t do it; just go in with your eyes open.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you moved from one home to another. What happened, and what did you learn from the experience?
t2.model:
A few years ago, I moved from a basement apartment into my first one-bedroom, and I thought I had everything planned perfectly. I’d packed for weeks and booked a moving company well in advance. But on the morning of the move, the elevator in my new building broke down, and I was on the eleventh floor.

The movers refused to carry everything up the stairs, so for about three hours my furniture just sat in the lobby. Eventually the superintendent got the elevator running again, but I paid extra for all that waiting time, and I was exhausted by the end of the day.

What I learned is that you should always have a backup plan and confirm every detail the day before. Now, whenever I help friends move, I tell them to call the building and check the elevator first.

scene.alt: A busy moving day outside a tall beige apartment building on a city street. On the left, a woman in an orange dress stands near the building’s brown front door and points toward the street. Beside her is a potted plant waiting to be moved. Two cardboard boxes are stacked on the sidewalk: the bottom one says BOOKS and the top one says FRAGILE, and it is sitting a little unevenly. In the middle, a man in a green shirt and a man in a red shirt with a dark cap are lifting a blue sofa together. A small girl in a red shirt is running toward the road holding the leash of a brown dog that has stepped off the curb. On the right, a white moving truck labelled QUICKMOVE is parked on the road next to a street lamp. A dark rain cloud is moving in from the right, while the rest of the sky has only a light cloud.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model:
This picture shows a moving day on a city street, right outside a tall beige apartment building. It looks like a fairly busy morning, and the sky is mostly clear, although there’s a dark rain cloud coming in on the right-hand side.

On the left, near the brown front door of the building, there’s a woman in an orange dress. She seems to be in charge, because she’s pointing toward the street, probably telling the movers where things should go. Next to her there’s a potted plant waiting on the sidewalk, and a couple of cardboard boxes stacked one on top of the other. The bottom one is labelled “BOOKS”, and the top one says “FRAGILE”, and to be honest, it doesn’t look very stable.

In the centre, two men are lifting a big blue sofa. One is wearing a green shirt, and the other has a red shirt and a dark cap. They’re carrying it toward a large white moving truck that’s parked on the road on the right, next to a street lamp.

Meanwhile, a little girl in a red shirt is running toward the road with a brown dog on a leash, and the dog has already stepped off the curb, which looks a bit dangerous with a truck parked right there.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model:
I think a few things will probably happen in the next few minutes.

First of all, that dark cloud on the right is moving in, so I expect it will start raining fairly soon. When the woman in the orange dress notices, she’ll probably shout at the two men to hurry, and they’ll rush to get the blue sofa into the truck before the fabric gets soaked. They might even bump into something because they’re moving too fast.

The boxes on the sidewalk are another problem. The fragile box on top is already sitting unevenly, so if someone brushes past it, or if the wind picks up before the rain, it could easily slide off and break whatever is inside. My guess is that the woman will grab it and carry it into the building lobby to keep it dry.

I’m also a bit worried about the little girl. The dog has already stepped onto the road, so I think her mother, or one of the movers, will call her back to the sidewalk and take the leash from her.

In the end, I imagine everyone will finish loading in a hurry, a little wet but with everything safely inside the truck.

t5.intro: You are moving to a new city for work and have found two apartments. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a family member that your choice is better than the one they prefer.
t5.persuade: Your sister prefers the room in a shared house. Persuade her that your choice is better.
t5.model:
I know the shared house looks like the obvious choice on paper, because $950 is a lot less than $1,750. But hear me out on the downtown studio.

First, think about time. I’d be ten minutes from work on foot, compared with a twenty-five-minute bus ride each way. That’s over three extra hours a week, and buses in a new city in winter can be unreliable. With the studio, I’d also save on a transit pass, which is easily over a hundred dollars a month, so the real gap is smaller than it looks.

Second, privacy. I’m starting a demanding new job, and I’ll need to rest properly. In a shared house, I’d be relying on three strangers to keep the kitchen clean and keep the noise down. Utilities split four ways sounds cheap until somebody leaves the heat on all winter and the others have to argue about it.

And I wouldn’t be missing out on space to relax. The studio has a rooftop terrace, which is a good substitute for a backyard, and a gym, so I could cancel a gym membership too.

So yes, the house is cheaper, but the studio gives me time, independence and peace of mind, which matter a lot when I’m settling in somewhere new.

t6.situation: You share a rented house with two roommates, Kenji and Tamsin. For the last two months, Kenji’s partner has been staying over almost every night. She uses the kitchen, laundry and showers, and the utility bills have gone up, but she does not contribute. Tamsin is upset and wants Kenji to start paying more. Kenji is your close friend from university, and you do not want to damage the friendship. The lease also says that only three people may live in the house.
options: Talk to Kenji and ask him to deal with the situation.
Talk to Tamsin and explain why you do not want to confront Kenji.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model:
Hey Kenji, have you got a few minutes? There’s something I’ve been meaning to bring up, and I’d rather talk about it face to face than let it get awkward.

First, I want to say that I really like Aiko, and I’m glad you two are happy. This isn’t about her as a person at all. It’s just that she’s been here almost every night for a couple of months now, and the house is set up for three people. The hydro and gas bills have gone up quite a bit, and Tamsin has noticed. She’s pretty frustrated, and I’d rather you hear that from me than have it blow up during a house meeting.

There’s also the lease. It says only three people can live here, and if the landlord decided Aiko was basically living here, it could actually cause problems for all of us.

So here’s what I’d suggest. Maybe Aiko could chip in a fair share of the utilities, say a quarter of the bills, while she’s staying over this much. Or, if she’s going to be here less often, that works too. I just think we should sort it out now, while it’s still a small thing. Would you be okay talking to her about it this week?

t7.prompt: Answer the following question: Should cities limit short-term vacation rentals in residential neighbourhoods so that more homes are available for long-term tenants? Explain your reasons.
t7.model:
In my opinion, yes, cities should limit short-term rentals, although I don’t think they should ban them completely.

My main reason is that housing is first and foremost a place for people to live. In many Canadian cities, vacancy rates are extremely low, and when an investor can earn more from tourists in a week than from a tenant in a month, it’s no surprise that apartments disappear from the long-term market. Every unit that becomes a full-time vacation rental is one less home for a nurse, a student or a young family.

Second, full-time short-term rentals can change the character of a neighbourhood. When half the units in a building have new guests every few days, neighbours stop knowing each other, and there are more problems with noise, garbage and security.

That said, I think a reasonable approach would be to allow people to rent out their own home, or a room in it, while they’re away, because that helps homeowners cover their costs without removing housing from the market. What cities should restrict are units that are used only as tourist accommodation all year.

So overall, I believe sensible limits would protect long-term tenants while still letting ordinary homeowners benefit.

scene.alt: An unusual vacation rental: a small, pale-orange cottage with a brown pointed roof, a door and windows, sitting on top of the cargo box of a white truck that is parked on a grassy field. The truck’s red cab is at the front, and the house fits neatly on top, as if the whole home could drive away. A short wooden ladder leans against the side so guests can climb up to the front door. A FOR RENT sign stands in the grass next to it. A man in a blue shirt is taking a photo of it with a camera, and a woman in a purple shirt stands next to him with a map. Mountains and pine trees are in the background, with clouds in the sky.

t8.prompt: You and your friend are looking for an unusual place to rent for a weekend getaway, and you have found this listing online. Call your friend, describe the place, and explain whether you think it would be a good choice. Your friend cannot see the picture.
t8.model:
Okay, you have to hear about this listing. I think I’ve found the most unusual place we could possibly stay. Picture a white truck, like a moving truck with a red cab, parked in a grassy field. Now, instead of a cargo box, on top of it there’s a whole little cottage. It’s pale orange with a brown pointed roof, a front door and windows, just like a tiny house. To get in, you climb up a short ladder leaning against the side.

The setting is gorgeous: mountains in the background, pine trees, wildflowers, and in the photo another couple is standing there taking pictures and looking at a map.

So, would it be a good choice? I honestly think yes, for one weekend. It would be a fun adventure, and the scenery looks perfect for hiking. My only concerns are space and comfort. The house can’t be much bigger than a small bedroom, so we’d need to pack light, and I’d want to check whether there’s a real bathroom. Also, the ladder might be tricky at night. But if the reviews are good, I say we book it. We’ll never forget it.
